newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish business heads accused of blackmail.
newsitem.headline: Swedish business heads accused of blackmail.

text.p: A Swedish minister accused business leaders on Friday of trying to blackmail the government, the latest salvo in an increasingly hostile war of words between the centre-left government and industry.

Stepping into the sixth day of a row between the business sector and Prime Minister Goran Persson, Industry and Commerce Minister Leif Pagrotsky dismissed criticism of the Social Democratic government's industrial policy. "The business sector's argument is so utterly predictable," Pagrotsky told Swedish reporters. "They say there is no dialogue but I've heard this argument a hundred times."

The row started when a letter signed by 101 heavyweight business leaders appeared in a weekend Swedish newspaper, attacking the Social Democrats who have traditionally worked closely with the nation's industrial sector.

The letter, signed by Lars Ramqvist of Ericsson, Soren Gyll of AB Volvo, Peter Wallenberg of Investor and ABB's Percy Barnevik, said the government was destroying industry confidence by agreeing to phase out nuclear power and increase public spending.
The minority government was also refusing to listen to the concerns of Swedish industry, they said.
Under an agreement signed with the Left and Centre parties this year the Social Democrats have agreed to close one of Sweden's 12 nuclear reactors in 1998 and a second in 2001.

Persson, celebrating a year in office next month, retorted by accusing the businessmen of playing politics and suggested record profits in recent years were paid for by the Swedish people through spending cuts.
Industry Minister Anders Sundstrom, in a press release, decried the inability of corporate leaders to recognise all of the positive signals in Sweden's business climate.
But economist Peter Lindqvist from Midland Bank said there was no doubt that the energy agreement had shaken confidence in the government.

Latest opinion polls show for the second straight month the conservative opposition, the Moderates, are ahead of the Social Democrats with 30.9 percent against 29.1 percent. The last time the Moderates were in front was in January 1996. "The polls clearly show confidence in the Social Democrats has been shaken due to the nuclear agreement," Lindqvist said.
The chairman of Sweden's largest bank, Handelbanken, Tom Hedelius, said some Swedish businesses may start moving head offices overseas unless the business climate at home improves.

"I don't like it when someone like Hedelius uses threats," Pagrotsky said. "In this case they are shooting themselves in the foot because we have lower company taxes in Sweden than in the countries they are talking about.

"They have forgotten what they spoke about a couple of years ago: inflation, the budget deficit and interest rates. Instead they have turned to other things that, as far as I can make out, are more to do with private economics."
Economist Peter Granqvist of Swedbank said the deterioration in the relationship between the business sector and the government should not hit financial markets in the short term.
"But if this were to escalate in some way ...it would be very unfortunate as it could damage confidence in the Swedish business sector and would affect investment confidence," Granqvist told Reuters.
Confederation of Industry chairman, Bert-Olof Svanholm said the business sector's concerns had fallen on deaf ears.
"It has been a long time since relations have been as bad as they are now," Svanholm said. 281013 GMT feb 97
